control-theory: In a PID controller, which term removes the steady-state error to a constant setpoint on a plant with no built-in integrator?
The integral term
The proportional term
The derivative term
The derivative filter
The integral term keeps growing while any error remains, so it drives the steady-state error to zero. Proportional action alone leaves a residual offset on such a plant.
A PID-controlled motor saturates at full voltage for several seconds, then overshoots badly once it nears the setpoint. What is the most likely cause?
Integral windup during saturation
Derivative kick from a setpoint step
Quantization noise in the encoder
Too much derivative filtering
While the output is saturated the integrator keeps accumulating error, and that stored value must unwind, causing overshoot. Anti-windup (clamping or back-calculation) fixes it.
A position loop tuned with P and I terms only oscillates with large overshoot. Which change most directly adds damping?
Add a moderate derivative term
Double the integral gain
Double the proportional gain
Lower the sample rate
The derivative term reacts to the rate of change of the error and opposes fast motion, which adds damping. Raising Ki or Kp generally makes overshoot worse.
Why do many PID implementations compute the derivative on the measurement instead of on the error?
To avoid a derivative kick when the setpoint steps
To remove the need for an integral term
To make the loop respond faster to setpoint steps
To reduce steady-state error to zero
A setpoint step makes the error jump instantly, so d(error)/dt spikes. Differentiating the measurement gives the same damping without that spike.
Why is the derivative term of a practical PID controller usually passed through a low-pass filter?
It amplifies high-frequency sensor noise
It accumulates error over long periods
It causes steady-state offset
It saturates the integrator
Differentiation boosts gain proportionally to frequency, so measurement noise is amplified. A first-order filter on the D term limits that high-frequency gain.
A discrete PI controller runs integral += e*dt, then u = Kp*e + Ki*integral, starting from integral = 0. With Kp = 2, Ki = 1, dt = 0.1 and e = 1 at every step, what is u after the 10th step?
After 10 steps the integral is 10 * 1 * 0.1 = 1.0, so u = 2 * 1 + 1 * 1.0 = 3.0.
A state-space model x' = Ax + Bu has 4 states and 2 inputs. What are the dimensions of B?
B maps the input vector (2 x 1) into the state derivative (4 x 1), so it must be 4 x 2.
When is a continuous-time LTI system x' = Ax asymptotically stable?
All eigenvalues of A have negative real parts
All eigenvalues of A lie inside the unit circle
The determinant of A is positive
All entries of A are negative
Each mode decays as exp(lambda t), which goes to zero only when Re(lambda) < 0. The unit-circle test applies to discrete-time systems.
For a system x' = Ax + Bu with n states, which condition means it is fully controllable?
The matrix [B, AB, ..., A^(n-1)B] has rank n
The matrix A has rank n
The matrix [C; CA; ...; CA^(n-1)] has rank n
The matrix B is square and invertible
The Kalman controllability test checks the rank of the controllability matrix. The stacked C, CA, ... matrix is the observability test instead.
A discrete-time system x[k+1] = A x[k] has eigenvalues 0.5 and -1.2. What can you conclude?
It is unstable because one eigenvalue has magnitude above 1
It is stable because the eigenvalues have opposite signs
It is stable because one eigenvalue is negative
It is marginally stable because the eigenvalues average below 1
In discrete time every eigenvalue must lie strictly inside the unit circle. The mode with magnitude 1.2 grows by 20 percent each step.
What does a continuous-time LQR controller minimize?
The integral of x'Qx + u'Ru over time
The peak overshoot of the step response
The settling time subject to input limits
The H-infinity norm of the closed loop
LQR finds the state feedback that minimizes a quadratic cost trading state error (weighted by Q) against control effort (weighted by R).
In an LQR design, you increase R while keeping Q fixed. What is the typical effect on the closed loop?
Smaller control effort and a slower response
Larger control effort and a faster response
Zero steady-state error to any setpoint
Loss of closed-loop stability
R penalizes control effort, so a larger R makes the optimizer use gentler inputs, which slows the response. Stability is still guaranteed under the usual LQR assumptions.
How is the gain K of an infinite-horizon LQR controller u = -Kx usually computed?
By solving the algebraic Riccati equation
By placing poles at chosen locations
By running a Ziegler-Nichols experiment
By inverting the controllability matrix
The steady-state Riccati equation gives the matrix P, and K = R^-1 B'P. Pole placement also gives a K, but not the one that minimizes the quadratic cost.
What does receding horizon mean in Model Predictive Control?
Optimize over a horizon, apply only the first input, then re-solve
Compute the whole input sequence once and play it back
Shrink the horizon by one step until the goal is reached
Use a fixed gain matrix computed offline for all steps
At each sample MPC solves an optimization over a finite future horizon, applies only the first control move, and repeats with the new measurement, which gives feedback.
Compared with LQR, what is the main practical advantage of Model Predictive Control?
It handles input and state limits directly
It needs no model of the plant
It is cheaper to compute at runtime
It guarantees zero noise sensitivity
MPC solves a constrained optimization online, so limits like actuator saturation or safe state bounds are part of the problem. LQR has no native way to impose them.
What is the main drawback of MPC on a fast embedded controller?
An optimization must be solved within every sample period
It cannot be used with multiple inputs
It only works for linear time-invariant plants
It requires a sensor for every state
MPC must finish solving its optimization before the next sample, which can be demanding at kHz rates. Nonlinear and MIMO versions exist, so those are not inherent limits.
On a Bode plot of the open-loop transfer function, where is the gain margin read?
At the frequency where the phase crosses -180 degrees
At the frequency where the gain crosses 0 dB
At the frequency where the gain peaks
At the lowest plotted frequency
Gain margin is how much the loop gain can rise before the magnitude reaches 0 dB at the phase crossover (-180 degrees). Phase margin is read at the 0 dB crossover.
An open-loop transfer function has a gain crossover where its phase is -135 degrees. What is the phase margin?
45 degrees
135 degrees
-45 degrees
225 degrees
Phase margin = 180 + phase at the gain crossover = 180 + (-135) = 45 degrees.
For an open-loop stable system, what does the Nyquist criterion say about closed-loop stability under unity negative feedback?
Stable if the Nyquist plot does not encircle the point -1
Stable if the Nyquist plot does not encircle the origin
Stable if the plot crosses the real axis only once
Stable if the plot stays inside the unit circle
With no open-loop right-half-plane poles (P = 0), the closed loop is stable when the number of encirclements of -1 is zero, since Z = N + P.
What is the magnitude slope of a pure integrator 1/s on a Bode plot?
-20 dB per decade
+20 dB per decade
-40 dB per decade
-10 dB per decade
|1/(j omega)| = 1/omega, which falls by a factor of 10 (20 dB) for every decade of frequency. A double integrator would give -40 dB per decade.
sensor-fusion: Under which assumptions is the standard Kalman filter the optimal estimator?
Linear models with Gaussian noise
Nonlinear models with uniform noise
Linear models with no process noise only
Any model as long as sensors are fast
With linear dynamics and Gaussian noise, the Kalman filter gives the minimum mean-square error estimate. For nonlinear models, variants such as the EKF or UKF are approximations.
How does the Extended Kalman Filter handle nonlinear motion and measurement models?
It linearizes them using Jacobians
It propagates a set of sigma points
It samples thousands of weighted particles
It ignores the nonlinear terms entirely
The EKF uses first-order Taylor expansions, computing Jacobians of f and h around the latest estimate. Sigma points belong to the UKF and particles to particle filters.
In the EKF prediction step P = F P F' + Q, what is F?
The Jacobian of the motion model
The Jacobian of the measurement model
The Kalman gain from the previous step
The measurement noise covariance
F linearizes the state transition f(x, u) around the current estimate so the covariance can be propagated. The measurement Jacobian H is used in the update step.
In a Kalman filter, you increase the measurement noise covariance R. What happens to the Kalman gain?
It decreases, so the filter trusts the prediction more
It increases, so the filter trusts the sensor more
It stays the same because R affects only P
It becomes negative and the filter diverges
The gain is roughly P / (P + R) in the scalar case, so a larger R shrinks it and new measurements move the estimate less.
A Kalman filter is configured with a process noise covariance Q that is far too small. What is the typical symptom?
It becomes overconfident and lags or ignores real changes
It becomes noisy and follows every sensor spike
It runs faster because P stays large
It turns into a moving average of the measurements
A tiny Q tells the filter its model is nearly perfect, so P shrinks and the gain drops. The estimate then fails to track real maneuvers and can diverge.
How does the Unscented Kalman Filter propagate uncertainty through a nonlinear function?
It passes deterministic sigma points through the function
It computes analytic Jacobians at the mean
It draws random particles and resamples them
It approximates the function with a lookup table
The unscented transform picks sigma points that capture the mean and covariance, maps each through the nonlinear function, and recombines them. No Jacobians are needed.
How many sigma points does the standard UKF use for an n-dimensional state?
2n
n squared
One sigma point sits at the mean and two lie symmetrically along each of the n directions of the covariance square root, giving 2n + 1.
Why might an engineer choose a UKF over an EKF for a strongly nonlinear model?
It is more accurate and needs no Jacobians
It is always cheaper per step than an EKF
It removes the need for a process noise model
It works without any model of the system
The unscented transform is accurate to at least second order for the mean, while the EKF is first order, and it avoids deriving Jacobians. It is usually somewhat more expensive.
In a Kalman filter update, what is the innovation (residual)?
The measurement minus the predicted measurement
The predicted state minus the previous state
The Kalman gain times the process noise
The trace of the covariance matrix
The innovation y = z - h(x_pred) is how much the measurement disagrees with the prediction. The update adds K times this residual to the state.
Why does a complementary filter for tilt combine a high-passed gyro angle with a low-passed accelerometer angle?
The gyro drifts slowly while the accelerometer is noisy at high frequency
The gyro is noisy at high frequency while the accelerometer drifts slowly
Both sensors drift, so their errors cancel when added
The accelerometer measures angular rate directly
Integrated gyro rate is smooth but accumulates bias drift, while the accelerometer gravity angle is drift-free but noisy. Each filter keeps the band where its sensor is reliable.
A complementary filter runs angle = 0.98 * (angle + gyro * dt) + 0.02 * accAngle. With angle = 10, gyro = 0, dt = 0.01 and accAngle = 20, what is the new angle?
0.98 * (10 + 0) + 0.02 * 20 = 9.8 + 0.4 = 10.2. The estimate moves only 2 percent of the way toward the accelerometer angle per step.
In the complementary filter angle = a * (angle + gyro * dt) + (1 - a) * accAngle, what happens if you raise a from 0.95 to 0.995?
The accelerometer corrects gyro drift more slowly
The gyro is ignored and accelerometer noise dominates
The filter stops integrating the gyro rate
The output becomes independent of dt
A larger a gives a longer time constant, tau = a * dt / (1 - a), so the gyro dominates longer and the accelerometer pulls the angle back more slowly.
An accelerometer-only tilt estimate on a car becomes wrong during hard braking. Why?
Linear acceleration adds to gravity in the measured vector
Braking changes the gyro bias
The magnetometer saturates during braking
Accelerometers cannot measure negative values
An accelerometer measures specific force, which equals gravity only when the body is not accelerating. Braking tilts the measured vector and corrupts the angle.
In a typical loosely coupled IMU + GPS Kalman filter, what role does each sensor play?
The IMU drives the high-rate prediction and GPS provides updates
GPS drives the high-rate prediction and the IMU provides updates
Both are fused only when GPS has fewer than four satellites
The IMU is used only to initialize the GPS receiver
IMU samples arrive at hundreds of Hz and propagate the state, while GPS position and velocity fixes at about 1 to 10 Hz correct the accumulated drift.
What is a key advantage of tightly coupled over loosely coupled GPS/INS integration?
It still helps with under four satellites
It needs no IMU bias estimation
It runs without any GPS receiver
It requires no time synchronization
Tightly coupled filters fuse raw pseudoranges and range rates, so even one to three satellites still constrain the solution. A loosely coupled filter needs a full GPS fix.
Why does position from a low-cost IMU alone drift so quickly?
Double integration makes a constant bias grow quadratically
Gyro noise cancels out the accelerometer readings
The IMU only measures position at a low rate
Gravity is removed perfectly, leaving no signal
Position comes from integrating acceleration twice, so a constant accelerometer bias b produces an error of about 0.5 * b * t^2.
A robot moving at 20 m/s fuses GPS fixes that are 100 ms old as if they were current. Roughly how large is the resulting position error?
2 m
The vehicle travels 20 m/s * 0.1 s = 2 m during the delay, so treating the stale fix as current misplaces it by about that much along the direction of travel.
GPS fixes reach your filter 200 ms after they were measured, while IMU data is near real time. Which approach handles this correctly?
Buffer past states, apply the fix at its timestamp, then re-propagate
Apply each fix immediately as if it were current, then continue
Discard every GPS fix older than one IMU sample period
Average each fix with the current IMU acceleration reading
Storing a history of states and IMU inputs lets the filter fuse the measurement at the moment it was taken, then replay the newer IMU data to reach the present.
Which GPS receiver output is commonly used to synchronize sensor clocks precisely?
The PPS signal
The GSV sentence
The HDOP value
The almanac data
The PPS pulse edge is aligned to the top of each GPS second with very low jitter, so it gives a precise time reference for timestamping other sensors.
How do many Kalman filters reject outlier measurements such as GPS multipath jumps?
Gate on the Mahalanobis distance of the innovation
Clamp the Kalman gain to exactly 1
Reset the covariance P to zero
Skip the prediction step for that sample
The innovation weighted by its covariance follows a chi-square distribution, so a measurement whose Mahalanobis distance exceeds a chosen threshold can be rejected.
embedded-c: Which C statement sets bit 3 of the register REG without changing any other bit?
OR with a mask sets only the masked bit. Plain assignment overwrites every other bit, and AND would clear all the others.
Which C statement clears bit 5 of REG and leaves all other bits unchanged?
AND with an inverted mask forces bit 5 to 0 and keeps every other bit. XOR would toggle bit 5, which sets it if it was already 0.
What is the value of (0xF0 >> 4) & 0x3 in C?
0xF0 >> 4 is 0x0F, and 0x0F & 0x03 keeps the two low bits, giving 3.
For uint8_t x = 0xA5, which expression extracts bits 7 to 4 as a value from 0 to 15?
x & 0xF0
Shifting right by 4 moves the upper nibble into bits 3 to 0, and the mask removes anything else, giving 0x0A here. x & 0xF0 keeps the nibble in place, yielding 0xA0.
Which line sets the 3-bit field in bits 6 to 4 of REG to the value 5 without touching other bits?
First clear the field with an inverted mask, then OR in the new value. REG |= (5U << 4) alone cannot clear bits that were already 1.
A flag set in an ISR is polled in while (!flag) {} in main, and the loop never exits with optimization on. What fixes it?
Declare the flag volatile
Declare the flag static
Declare the flag const
Declare the flag register
Without volatile the compiler may read the flag once and keep it in a register, since nothing in the loop changes it. volatile forces a fresh memory read each time.
On an 8-bit AVR, main reads a volatile uint32_t counter that an ISR increments. Occasionally it reads a corrupted value. Why?
The 4-byte read is not atomic and the ISR can fire midway
volatile disables the ISR during the read
The compiler caches the counter in a register
uint32_t is not supported on 8-bit MCUs
An 8-bit CPU reads the counter one byte at a time, so an interrupt between bytes mixes old and new values. volatile does not make access atomic; briefly disable interrupts while reading.
Which definition correctly gives access to a 32-bit hardware register at address 0x40021018?
#define REG (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40021018)
#define REG ((volatile uint32_t)0x40021018)
#define REG (*(uint32_t volatile **)0x40021018)
#define REG (&(volatile uint32_t *)0x40021018)
Casting the address to a pointer to volatile uint32_t and dereferencing it gives an lvalue that reads and writes the register. The first wrong option is just a number, not a memory access.
What is the difference between volatile uint32_t *p and uint32_t * volatile p?
The first makes the pointed-to data volatile, the second the pointer itself
The first makes the pointer volatile, the second the pointed-to data
They are identical declarations with different spelling
The first is read-only, the second is write-only
Qualifiers apply to what is on their left, or to the right if nothing is left. For memory-mapped I/O you want the data volatile, as in volatile uint32_t *p.
What is the recommended pattern for heavy processing triggered by an interrupt?
Set a flag or queue data in the ISR, process it in the main loop
Do all processing in the ISR so it runs immediately
Call printf in the ISR to log the event first
Disable all interrupts globally inside the main loop
Short ISRs keep interrupt latency low for other sources. Deferring the work avoids blocking calls and long critical sections inside interrupt context.
An STM32 timer ISR keeps executing over and over and main never runs. What is the most likely cause?
The ISR does not clear the timer's update interrupt flag
The timer prescaler is set too high
The ISR is missing the volatile keyword
The main loop has no infinite loop
If the pending flag in the peripheral is not cleared, the interrupt is requested again as soon as the ISR returns, so the CPU re-enters it continuously.
On an ARM Cortex-M NVIC, which interrupt is serviced first when two configurable interrupts are pending?
The one with the lower numeric priority value
The one with the higher numeric priority value
The one with the higher IRQ number
The one that became pending last
On Cortex-M a lower priority number means higher urgency, so priority 1 preempts priority 5. With equal priority, the lower exception number wins.
Why does STM32 GPIO provide the BSRR register in addition to ODR?
To set or reset pins atomically without a read-modify-write
To read the input level of each pin
To configure pins as analog inputs
To select the alternate function of a pin
Writing a 1 to a BSRR bit sets or resets one pin in a single write, so an ISR modifying other pins cannot be overwritten by a concurrent ODR |= in main.
A timer is clocked at 72 MHz with prescaler register PSC = 71 and auto-reload ARR = 999. What is the update event frequency?
1 kHz
1 MHz
72 kHz
100 Hz
A timer in edge-aligned PWM mode 1 has ARR = 999. Which compare value CCR gives a 25 percent duty cycle?
The period is ARR + 1 = 1000 counts and the output is high while the counter is below CCR, so CCR = 250 gives 250 / 1000 = 25 percent.
With a fixed timer clock, you raise the PWM frequency by lowering the auto-reload value. What else changes?
The duty-cycle resolution gets coarser
The duty-cycle resolution gets finer
The PWM output voltage gets higher
The timer clock frequency gets higher
The number of counts per period equals ARR + 1, and that is also the number of possible duty steps. Fewer counts per period means fewer steps.
What does the WFI instruction do on an ARM Cortex-M core?
Puts the core to sleep until an interrupt occurs
Waits until a flag variable becomes 1
Resets the core and restarts the firmware
Disables all interrupts until the next reset
Wait For Interrupt stops the core clock to save power, and any enabled interrupt wakes it. Deeper modes are selected by also setting SLEEPDEEP in the System Control Register.
On an STM32 microcontroller, how does the firmware resume after waking from Standby mode?
It restarts from the reset vector, as after a reset
It continues from the instruction after WFI
It continues from the last ISR that ran
It resumes from a snapshot stored in flash
Standby powers down most of the chip and loses SRAM and register contents (apart from the backup domain), so wake-up behaves like a reset. Sleep and Stop modes resume after WFI.
Which practice most directly reduces current draw in a battery-powered microcontroller application?
Disable clocks to peripherals that are not in use
Raise the core clock to the maximum
Poll inputs in a tight loop instead of sleeping
Leave unused pins as floating digital inputs
Each clocked peripheral draws dynamic current, so gating unused clocks saves power. Floating digital inputs can toggle on noise and draw extra current.
In C, after uint8_t x = 0x80; x = x << 1; what is the value of x?
0xFF
x is promoted to int, so x << 1 is 0x100, but storing it back in a uint8_t keeps only the low 8 bits, which are 0x00.
arduino: How do setup() and loop() behave in an Arduino sketch?
setup() runs once after reset, then loop() repeats forever
loop() runs once, then setup() repeats forever
Both run once in order and the board halts
Both run in parallel on separate threads
The Arduino core calls setup() once at power-up or reset, then calls loop() repeatedly for as long as the board is powered.
Inside loop() you write: int count = 0; count++; Serial.println(count); What does the Serial Monitor show?
1 on every iteration
1, 2, 3 and so on
0 on every iteration
A compile error
count is a local variable re-created and set to 0 on every call to loop(), so it is always 1 when printed. Making it static or global would make it accumulate.
What range of values does analogRead() return on an Arduino Uno?
The ATmega328P ADC is 10-bit, so readings range from 0 to 1023. 0 to 255 is the default range of analogWrite().
On an Uno with the default 5 V reference, analogRead() returns 512. Approximately what voltage is on the pin?
Voltage is about reading * 5 V / 1024, so 512 corresponds to roughly 2.5 V.
What does analogWrite(9, 127) produce on an Arduino Uno?
A PWM signal with about 50 percent duty cycle
A steady voltage of about 2.5 V
A 127 Hz square wave
A 127 mV analog voltage
The Uno has no DAC, so analogWrite() outputs PWM on pins marked with a tilde. 127 of 255 is about half duty; it averages to 2.5 V only after filtering.
A button connects digital pin 2 to GND, and the pin is set with pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP). What does digitalRead(2) return while the button is pressed?
LOW
HIGH
A random value
It depends on the baud rate
The internal pull-up holds the pin HIGH when the button is open; pressing it connects the pin to ground, so it reads LOW.
The Serial Monitor shows garbled characters after Serial.begin(115200) in the sketch. What is the most likely fix?
Set the Serial Monitor baud rate to 115200
Change the USB cable to a shorter one
Add delay(1000) after every print
Use Serial.write() instead of Serial.print()
Both ends of a UART link must use the same baud rate. If the monitor is set to 9600 while the board sends at 115200, the bytes decode as garbage.
What is the difference between Serial.print(x) and Serial.println(x)?
println() also sends a carriage return and newline
println() sends the value in binary format
println() waits for an acknowledgment
println() clears the receive buffer first
Both print the value as text, but println() appends a carriage return and line feed so the next output starts on a new line.
What does Serial.available() return?
The number of bytes waiting in the receive buffer
Whether the USB cable is connected
The configured baud rate
The number of free bytes in the transmit buffer
It returns how many received bytes can be read right now, so code typically checks if (Serial.available() > 0) before calling Serial.read().
Uploading a sketch to an Uno fails while a Bluetooth module is wired to pins 0 and 1. Why?
Pins 0 and 1 are the UART that USB uploads use
Pins 0 and 1 are reserved for the reset circuit
Pins 0 and 1 are only analog inputs
The bootloader disables pins 0 and 1
On the Uno, pins 0 (RX) and 1 (TX) share the hardware serial port with the USB-to-serial chip, so another device driving RX interferes with uploading.
Which call correctly attaches an interrupt to a button on pin 2 of an Uno, triggering when the pin goes from HIGH to LOW?
attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(2), onPress, FALLING);
attachInterrupt(2, onPress, LOW_TO_HIGH);
attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(2), onPress, RISING);
attachInterrupt(onPress, 2, FALLING);
digitalPinToInterrupt() maps the pin to its interrupt number, and FALLING triggers on a HIGH to LOW edge. RISING triggers on the opposite edge.
Which digital pins on an Arduino Uno support attachInterrupt()?
Pins 2 and 3
Pins 0 and 1
Pins 10 to 13
All digital pins
The ATmega328P has two external interrupt lines, INT0 and INT1, on digital pins 2 and 3. Other pins only have pin-change interrupts, which attachInterrupt() does not use.
What happens to millis() while code is running inside an ISR on an Arduino Uno?
Its value does not advance
It advances twice as fast
It resets to zero
It returns a negative number
millis() is updated by a timer interrupt, which cannot run while another ISR is executing, so it will not increment inside the ISR. delay() also does not work there.
How should a global variable that an ISR changes and loop() reads be declared?
As volatile
As const
As static inside loop()
As a #define macro
volatile tells the compiler the value can change outside the normal flow, so it reloads it from memory instead of using a cached copy.
On an Arduino Uno, using the standard Servo library disables analogWrite() on which pins?
Pins 9 and 10
Pins 5 and 6
Pins 3 and 11
Pins 0 and 1
On non-Mega boards the Servo library uses Timer1, which drives the PWM on pins 9 and 10. Pins 5 and 6 use Timer0 and pins 3 and 11 use Timer2.
What is an Arduino shield?
A board that plugs onto the headers to add hardware
A firmware layer that protects the bootloader
A plastic case that protects the board
A library that blocks pin conflicts
Shields stack onto the standard header layout to add features such as motor drivers, Ethernet or displays, usually with a companion library.
Why is it risky to change the prescaler of Timer0 on an Arduino Uno?
millis() and delay() depend on Timer0
Timer0 drives the USB serial chip
Timer0 controls the ADC reference
Timer0 is needed by the bootloader
The Arduino core uses Timer0 overflow interrupts for millis(), micros() and delay(), so changing its prescaler distorts all timing functions.
On the ATmega328P used in the Arduino Uno, which timer is 16-bit?
Timer1
Timer0
Timer2
Timer3
Timer0 and Timer2 are 8-bit, and Timer1 is the only 16-bit timer. The ATmega328P has no Timer3; that exists on chips like the ATmega2560.
Timer1 on a 16 MHz Uno runs in CTC mode with a prescaler of 256. Which OCR1A value gives a 1 Hz compare interrupt?
The timer ticks at 16,000,000 / 256 = 62,500 Hz, and in CTC mode the period is OCR1A + 1 ticks, so OCR1A = 62,500 - 1 = 62,499.
Which code avoids a bug when millis() overflows after about 49.7 days?
if (millis() - start >= interval)
if (millis() >= start + interval)
if (millis() > interval)
if (start + millis() >= interval)
Unsigned subtraction wraps correctly, so the elapsed time is right across the overflow. Comparing millis() to start + interval fails when that sum wraps around.
raspberry-pi: What logic level do Raspberry Pi GPIO pins use?
3.3 V, and they are not 5 V tolerant
5 V, and they are 3.3 V compatible
1.8 V, and they are 3.3 V tolerant
12 V, matching typical motor drivers
Raspberry Pi GPIO operates at 3.3 V. Applying 5 V to an input can permanently damage the SoC, so 5 V signals need a level shifter or divider.
On the 40-pin Raspberry Pi header, physical pin 11 corresponds to which BCM GPIO number?
GPIO17
GPIO11
GPIO27
GPIO4
BOARD numbering counts physical header pins, while BCM numbering uses the SoC GPIO numbers. Physical pin 11 is BCM GPIO17.
What is the right way to run a 12 V DC motor from a Raspberry Pi GPIO pin?
Use a motor driver or MOSFET with a separate supply
Connect the motor directly between GPIO and GND
Power the motor from the 3.3 V pin
Use a resistor in series with the motor
A GPIO pin can only source a few milliamps at 3.3 V. A driver switches the motor current from its own supply, and a flyback diode protects against inductive spikes.
Using the gpiozero library, which code turns on an LED connected to BCM GPIO17?
led = LED(17); led.on()
led = LED(11); led.on()
led = LED(17); led.high()
led = LED("P17"); led.start()
gpiozero uses BCM numbering by default, and the LED class has on(), off() and toggle(). Pin 11 is the physical number of GPIO17, not its BCM number.
Which Linux interface replaces the deprecated sysfs GPIO interface (/sys/class/gpio)?
The GPIO character device, used through libgpiod
The /proc/gpio virtual file
Direct writes to /dev/mem only
The /sys/bus/i2c driver directory
Since Linux 4.8, GPIO lines are exposed as /dev/gpiochipN character devices, and libgpiod tools such as gpioset and gpioget use them. sysfs GPIO is kept only for compatibility.
In the legacy sysfs GPIO interface, after a pin is exported as gpioN, which file do you write "out" to in order to make it an output?
/sys/class/gpio/gpioN/direction
/sys/class/gpio/gpioN/value
/sys/class/gpio/gpioN/edge
/sys/class/gpio/export
The direction file accepts "in" or "out". The value file then reads or sets the level, and edge configures interrupt triggering for inputs.
Which command scans I2C bus 1 on a Raspberry Pi and shows the addresses of connected devices?
i2cdetect -y 1
i2cdump -y 1
lsusb -t
spidev_test -D 1
i2cdetect from i2c-tools probes each 7-bit address on the bus and prints a grid of responding devices. i2cdump reads registers from one known device.
You connect three sensors to a Raspberry Pi over SPI. What does SPI need for this that I2C does not?
A separate chip select line for each device
A unique 7-bit address for each device
Pull-up resistors on every line
A separate clock frequency per device
SPI devices share clock and data lines, and the master picks one with its chip select (CE) line. I2C instead selects devices by address on two shared wires.
A Raspberry Pi UART is wired to an Arduino Uno. What must you add between Uno TX and Pi RX?
A level shifter or divider down to 3.3 V
A pull-up resistor to 5 V
A capacitor to filter the data
Nothing, since UART is voltage independent
The Uno drives 5 V logic and the Pi input is not 5 V tolerant. TX and RX must also be crossed and the grounds connected.
Where do you enable the SPI, I2C or serial interfaces on Raspberry Pi OS from a terminal?
sudo raspi-config, under Interface Options
sudo systemctl enable spi-i2c
sudo apt install interfaces
sudo nano /etc/hostname
raspi-config writes the needed dtparam lines to the boot configuration file and loads the drivers. A reboot may be required afterward.
On a Raspberry Pi 3 or 4 with Bluetooth enabled, which UART is mapped to GPIO14 and GPIO15 by default?
The mini UART
The PL011 UART
The USB UART
The SPI UART
The full PL011 UART is assigned to Bluetooth, so the header gets the mini UART, whose baud rate depends on the core clock. A device tree overlay can swap them.
Which Python library is the official camera interface for the libcamera stack on Raspberry Pi OS Bullseye and later?
Picamera2
picamera
pygame.camera
PiCam-Lite
Picamera2 is built on libcamera. The original picamera library depended on the legacy camera stack and does not work with libcamera.
Through which interface does the official Raspberry Pi Camera Module connect to the board?
MIPI CSI
MIPI DSI
SPI
USB 2.0
The camera ribbon plugs into the CSI connector. The similar-looking DSI connector is for displays, so the cable must go into the correct one.
Which CPU does the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B use?
A quad-core ARM Cortex-A72
A quad-core Intel Atom
A dual-core ARM Cortex-M4
A single-core RISC-V
The Pi 4 uses the Broadcom BCM2711 SoC with four 64-bit Cortex-A72 cores. Cortex-M parts are microcontrollers, not application processors.
A Raspberry Pi 4 without network access shows the wrong date and time after every reboot. Why?
It has no battery-backed real-time clock
Its CPU clock resets after every reboot
The SD card stores time in UTC only
Its GPIO pins disable the system clock
The Pi 4 has no RTC, so it gets time over the network via NTP. Without a network it falls back to a saved time, so an external RTC module is needed offline.
How do you read an analog potentiometer with a Raspberry Pi?
Use an external ADC such as the MCP3008 over SPI
Call analogRead() on any GPIO pin
Read the voltage from /sys/class/gpio
Configure a GPIO pin as an analog input
The Raspberry Pi has no built-in ADC, so analog signals need an external converter. The MCP3008 is a common 10-bit, 8-channel SPI ADC.
What is a common cause of microSD card corruption on a Raspberry Pi?
Cutting power while the system is writing
Using SPI and I2C at the same time
Running the CPU at its stock frequency
Enabling SSH on the first boot
Removing power mid-write can leave the file system inconsistent. Use sudo shutdown before unplugging, and consider a read-only root or a UPS for embedded setups.
For a headless setup, which file can you create on the boot partition so that SSH is enabled on first boot?
An empty file named ssh
A file named enable_ssh.conf
A file named sshd_config.txt
A file named authorized_ssh
At boot, Raspberry Pi OS checks for a file named ssh (or ssh.txt) on the boot partition, enables the SSH server and deletes the file. Raspberry Pi Imager settings can do the same.
What changed about the default user in Raspberry Pi OS releases from April 2022 onward?
There is no default pi user; you create one at setup
The default user became root with no password
The default password changed to admin
Logins became possible only through VNC
To improve security, the fixed pi / raspberry account was removed. The username and password are now set in the first-boot wizard or in Raspberry Pi Imager.
Which power supply does Raspberry Pi recommend for the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B?
5 V, 3 A over USB-C
5 V, 1 A over micro-USB
12 V, 2 A over a barrel jack
3.3 V, 3 A over GPIO
The official Pi 4 supply is 5.1 V at 3 A through USB-C. A weak supply causes undervoltage warnings and throttling.
jetson: In NVIDIA JetPack, what is Jetson Linux (formerly L4T)?
The BSP: kernel, bootloader and Ubuntu root file system
A cloud service for training models before deployment
A Python library for reading CSI cameras
A desktop GPU driver for x86 workstations
Jetson Linux is the BSP at the base of JetPack. CUDA, cuDNN, TensorRT and other libraries are installed on top of it.
Which command shows the Jetson Linux (L4T) release installed on a Jetson device?
cat /etc/nv_tegra_release
nvcc --l4t-version
cat /proc/jetpack
lsmod | grep tegra
The /etc/nv_tegra_release file records the L4T release and revision, which maps to a specific JetPack version.
How does memory on a Jetson module differ from a desktop with a discrete NVIDIA GPU?
The CPU and GPU share the same physical DRAM
The GPU has its own dedicated GDDR memory
The GPU cannot access system memory
The CPU accesses memory only through PCIe
Jetson SoCs integrate the GPU and share one LPDDR memory pool. Copies between host and device buffers still move data within the same DRAM, so zero-copy designs can avoid them.
On a Jetson, which CUDA allocation lets both CPU and GPU access the same buffer without explicit cudaMemcpy calls?
cudaMallocManaged
cudaMalloc
cudaMallocPitch
cudaMemcpyToSymbol
Managed (unified) memory gives one pointer usable from host and device. cudaMalloc returns device-only memory that the CPU cannot dereference.
Which built-in Jetson utility prints live CPU, GPU (GR3D) and memory usage along with power rails?
tegrastats
nvidia-settings
glxinfo
lspci -v
tegrastats ships with Jetson Linux and reports per-core CPU load, GR3D GPU load, RAM use, temperatures and, on many modules, power.
Which command shows the current power mode on a Jetson?
sudo nvpmodel -q
sudo nvpmodel -m 0 --dry
sudo jetson_clocks --mode
sudo tegrastats -p
nvpmodel -q queries the active power mode, and nvpmodel -m N switches to mode N as defined in /etc/nvpmodel.conf.
What does sudo jetson_clocks do?
Locks clocks at the current power mode maximum
Switches the board to the lowest power mode
Resets all clocks to their boot defaults
Overclocks the GPU beyond the mode limits
jetson_clocks pins clocks at the highest frequency allowed by the active nvpmodel mode, which removes DVFS ramp-up delays. It does not exceed the mode's limits.
What does selecting a lower power budget mode with nvpmodel typically change on a Jetson?
It caps CPU and GPU frequencies and may take CPU cores offline
It switches the GPU to FP64 precision
It disables the CUDA runtime entirely
It lowers the memory size reported to Linux
Each nvpmodel mode defines a power budget through the number of online CPU cores and maximum CPU, GPU and memory clocks.
Which nvcc flag targets the GPU in a Jetson AGX Orin?
-arch=sm_87
-arch=sm_72
-arch=sm_53
-arch=sm_86
Jetson Orin has compute capability 8.7. sm_72 is Jetson Xavier, sm_53 is the original Jetson Nano, and sm_86 is desktop Ampere GPUs.
On which multimedia framework are NVIDIA DeepStream SDK pipelines built?
GStreamer
FFmpeg
OpenMAX IL only
DirectShow
DeepStream provides GStreamer plugins (nvstreammux, nvinfer, nvtracker and others), so pipelines are assembled from GStreamer elements.
In a DeepStream pipeline, which plugin runs neural network inference using TensorRT?
nvinfer
nvstreammux
nvdsosd
nvvideoconvert
Gst-nvinfer loads a TensorRT engine and attaches detection or classification metadata. nvstreammux batches inputs and nvdsosd draws overlays.
A DeepStream app processes four camera streams with one model. Which plugin batches frames from the sources before inference?
nvstreammux
nvinfer
nvtracker
nvmsgbroker
nvstreammux combines frames from multiple sources into one batch so nvinfer can run them together efficiently.
In DeepStream, which plugin assigns persistent IDs to detected objects across frames?
nvtracker
nvinfer
nvstreammux
nvdsosd
nvtracker associates detections over time and gives each object a tracking ID, which is needed for counting or trajectory analysis.
Which GStreamer source element captures from a MIPI CSI camera through the Jetson ISP?
nvarguscamerasrc
v4l2src
videotestsrc
filesrc
nvarguscamerasrc uses the libargus camera stack and the hardware ISP for debayering. v4l2src is typically used for USB cameras.
Which GStreamer source element reads frames from a USB webcam exposed as /dev/video0 on a Jetson?
v4l2src device=/dev/video0
nvarguscamerasrc sensor-id=0
udpsrc port=0
appsrc name=video0
USB UVC cameras appear as V4L2 devices, so v4l2src reads them. nvarguscamerasrc is for CSI sensors handled by the ISP.
What is a main advantage of a MIPI CSI camera over a USB camera on a Jetson?
It uses the onboard ISP, lowering CPU load and latency
It needs no driver or device tree support
It works on any computer without changes
It can be hot-plugged while the board runs
CSI sensors feed the hardware ISP directly, which handles debayering and processing. CSI sensors usually need a matching driver and device tree entry.
Which command builds a TensorRT engine from an ONNX model and saves it?
trtexec --onnx=model.onnx --saveEngine=model.engine
trtexec --engine=model.onnx --save=model.trt
nvcc --onnx model.onnx -o model.engine
tensorrt build model.onnx model.engine
trtexec ships with TensorRT; --onnx parses the model and --saveEngine serializes the optimized engine for later loading.
A TensorRT engine built on a desktop RTX GPU fails to load on a Jetson. What is the correct fix?
Rebuild the engine on the Jetson from the ONNX model
Rename the engine file extension to .plan
Copy the desktop CUDA libraries to the Jetson
Convert the engine to FP32 with a script
Serialized TensorRT engines are tied to the GPU model and TensorRT version they were built with. Keep the ONNX model and build the engine on the target.
What extra step does TensorRT need to run a model trained in FP32 at INT8 precision with good accuracy?
Calibration on representative input data
Retraining the model from scratch in FP16
Removing all convolution layers first
Converting the model to TensorFlow Lite
INT8 needs a scale for each tensor. TensorRT finds them by calibrating on sample inputs, or reads them from a QAT model with quantize and dequantize nodes.
On Jetson Xavier or AGX Orin, what does trtexec --useDLACore=0 --allowGPUFallback do?
Runs supported layers on DLA 0 and the rest on the GPU
Runs the whole model on CPU core 0
Disables the GPU and uses only the CPU
Runs layers on DLA 0 and drops unsupported ones
The Deep Learning Accelerator supports a subset of layers. With GPU fallback enabled, unsupported layers run on the GPU instead of causing the build to fail.
fpga: How many configuration bits does a 6-input LUT store?
A k-input LUT stores one output bit for each of the 2^k input combinations, so a 6-input LUT holds 2^6 = 64 bits.
How does a LUT in an FPGA implement a Boolean function?
It stores the truth table in memory cells
It wires together fixed AND and OR gates
It runs the function on a tiny CPU
It uses analog comparators on the inputs
The LUT inputs act as an address into SRAM cells holding the truth table, so any function of its inputs can be implemented.
What does the Verilog code always @(posedge clk) q <= d; infer?
A D flip-flop
A level-sensitive latch
A combinational multiplexer
A tristate buffer
Assigning on a clock edge creates an edge-triggered register that captures d on each rising edge of clk.
In Verilog, always @(*) if (en) q = d; has no else branch. What does synthesis infer?
A latch
A D flip-flop
A multiplexer with zero default
A synthesis error
When en is 0, q must keep its old value, which requires storage without a clock, so the tool infers a latch. Add an else or a default assignment.
What does always @(posedge clk) begin a <= b; b <= a; end do in Verilog?
Swaps a and b on every rising clock edge
Copies b into both a and b
Copies a into both a and b
Causes a race and is not synthesizable
Non-blocking assignments read all right-hand sides first and update together, so the registers swap. With blocking = both would end up equal.
What is the setup time of a flip-flop?
How long data must be stable before the clock edge
How long data must be stable after the clock edge
The delay from the clock edge to a valid output
The minimum width of the clock high phase
If data changes within the setup window before the edge, the flip-flop may capture a wrong or metastable value. Stability after the edge is the hold time.
How should a single-bit asynchronous signal be safely brought into a new clock domain?
Through a two-flip-flop synchronizer
Through a single combinational buffer
By sampling it on both clock edges
By adding a longer wire delay
The first flop may go metastable, and the second gives it a full cycle to resolve, sharply reducing the chance of failure downstream.
What is the standard way to move a multi-bit data stream between two unrelated clock domains?
An asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers
A two-flop synchronizer on every data bit
A shared register read on both clocks
A combinational path with a false path constraint
The FIFO lets each side work in its own clock. Gray-coded pointers change one bit at a time, so they can be synchronized safely for the full and empty flags.
Why is synchronizing each bit of a binary counter separately with two-flop synchronizers unsafe?
Bits may settle on different clock cycles
Two-flop synchronizers only work on clock signals
Synthesis tools reject buses in synchronizers
It doubles the counter's clock frequency
When several bits change at once, each synchronizer can capture old or new data independently, so the received value may never have existed.
A design meets timing after synthesis but fails after place and route. What is the most likely reason?
Real routing delays exceed the synthesis estimates
The bitstream was generated before routing
Synthesis ignored the clock constraint
The simulation testbench was too short
Synthesis only estimates net delays. After placement and routing, actual wire lengths and congestion are known, and long routes can push paths past the clock period.
A long combinational path fails timing at the target clock. Which change most directly fixes it?
Insert pipeline registers to split the path
Remove the clock constraint for that path
Add a latch at the end of the path
Lower the I/O drive strength
Pipelining divides the logic into shorter stages that each fit within one clock period, at the cost of added latency.
A Vivado timing report shows a negative WNS (worst negative slack) for a clock. What does that mean?
At least one path misses its timing
The design runs faster than the constraint
The clock is not constrained at all
The design has no paths on that clock
Slack is required time minus arrival time. A negative WNS means the worst path arrives late, so the design is not guaranteed to work at that frequency.
How does synthesis treat a delay such as #10 in Verilog RTL code?
It ignores the delay
It inserts a 10 ns buffer chain
It adds 10 flip-flops in series
It reports a fatal error
Delays are a simulation construct only. Hardware timing comes from the real gates and routing, which is why simulation-only delays can hide bugs.
A combinational always block lists only some inputs in its sensitivity list, such as always @(a). What is a likely result?
Simulation and synthesized hardware behave differently
Synthesis infers a flip-flop clocked by a
Synthesis removes the missing inputs from the logic
The design runs at twice the clock rate
Synthesis builds logic from the code, ignoring the incomplete list, while the simulator only re-evaluates when a changes. Use always @(*) to avoid the mismatch.
What happens to an SRAM-based FPGA's configuration when power is removed?
It is lost and reloaded from flash
It is kept permanently in the LUT memory
It is restored from the last simulation
It is stored in the JTAG cable
SRAM configuration cells are volatile, so the bitstream is usually kept in SPI flash and loaded on each power-up. Flash and antifuse FPGAs are non-volatile.
In the AMD Vivado flow, which order is correct?
Synthesis, implementation, bitstream generation
Implementation, synthesis, bitstream generation
Bitstream generation, synthesis, implementation
Synthesis, bitstream generation, implementation
Synthesis maps RTL to a netlist, implementation places and routes it on the device, and the bitstream is generated from the routed design.
Which XDC command defines a 100 MHz clock on the input port clk?
create_clock -period 10 [get_ports clk]
create_clock -period 100 [get_ports clk]
set_input_delay -clock 100 [get_ports clk]
create_clock -freq 10 [get_ports clk]
create_clock takes the period in nanoseconds, and 1 / 100 MHz = 10 ns. Without it, timing analysis does not know the target frequency.
Two unrelated clocks cross only through proper synchronizers. Which constraint tells the timing tools not to analyze paths between them?
set_clock_groups -asynchronous
set_input_delay -clock
create_generated_clock
set_multicycle_path 2
Declaring the clocks asynchronous removes meaningless cross-domain timing checks. set_multicycle_path relaxes paths between related clocks rather than removing them.
What does set_input_delay model in an XDC or SDC constraint file?
Delay of external logic before data reaches an input port
Delay added inside the FPGA by an IDELAY block
Delay between two internal flip-flops
Delay of the clock buffer tree
set_input_delay tells the tool how much of the clock period is used outside the FPGA, so it can check the remaining internal path from the input port.
Which XDC property assigns a top-level port to a physical package pin?
PACKAGE_PIN
IOSTANDARD
DRIVE
SLEW
set_property PACKAGE_PIN E3 [get_ports clk] places the port on pin E3. IOSTANDARD sets the voltage standard, such as LVCMOS33, but not the location.
